_comment: Single source of truth. The site builds its navigation from this file; SCOUT rotates categories through it; the schema's category enum must match these slugs. Adding a domain or subcategory is a human decision (PRINCIPLES §6).

domains.name: Kitchen & Cooking
domains.problem: Large kitchen appliances are the hardest category to shop honestly: manufacturers mix connected and non-connected versions inside one model line with no naming convention that tells them apart, so the model number is the only thing that answers the question. Small appliances are easier, and commercial food-service equipment is easier still — a kitchen cannot have staff learning a menu system.

domains.name: Laundry & Cleaning
domains.blurb: Washers, dryers, vacuums, and floor care.
domains.problem: Washers and dryers last long enough that a cloud dependency contracted today is a problem for the 2040s. The commercial-derived machines are the reliable answer here: laundromat operators will not buy equipment that stops working when a vendor's server does, and that requirement keeps mechanical controls in production.

domains.name: Climate & Air
domains.problem: Thermostats are a bright spot. The non-connected models are cheap, widely sold, and sit right next to their Wi-Fi siblings on the same shelf — so the only thing standing between you and a thermostat that will never need an account is knowing the model number.

domains.name: Lighting & Electrical
domains.problem: The cheapest, most reliable automation in this category is a clockwork dial that costs less than a smart bulb and cannot be discontinued. Where you do want addressable control, prefer a local protocol with a hub you own over anything that pairs to a manufacturer's account.

domains.name: Security & Access
domains.problem: The category with the most to lose. Cameras, locks and openers are exactly where a vendor's decision to shut down a server or revoke an API has the sharpest consequences, and several have done it. Prefer ONVIF cameras with a recorder you own, and openers whose wall button was never in question.

domains.name: Automotive
domains.blurb: Dashcams, head units, and everything in the car.
domains.problem: Dashcams split cleanly: the ones that write to an SD card and the ones that want a subscription. Cellular and cloud models charge monthly for storage you could hold in your hand, and several vendors have made the app the only way to change a setting. The good news is that this is one of the few categories where the dumb option is also the cheaper and better-performing one.

domains.name: Audio & Video
domains.problem: Televisions are nearly a lost category. Every major brand has stopped selling consumer sets without a smart platform, and the platform is increasingly the product: home screens sell placement, and some sets analyse what is on screen. What remains is small non-smart panels, commercial signage displays, or buying a smart set and never giving it Wi-Fi.

domains.name: Computing & Networking
domains.problem: Printers are the worst offenders on this site. Manufacturers have shipped firmware that disables third-party cartridges on machines customers already owned, gated ink behind subscriptions, and made accounts mandatory to finish setup. The reliable escape is a printer with no network interface at all — if it cannot reach the manufacturer, none of this can happen to it.

domains.name: Cameras & Optics
domains.problem: Trail cameras divide on cellular versus SD card, and the SD card side wins on almost every axis: no subscription, no account, and batteries that last months instead of weeks because nothing is powering a radio.

domains.name: Health & Personal Care
domains.problem: Measurement is the product. A monitor that cannot show you a reading without a phone is a worse instrument, not a smarter one — so the test here is whether the number appears on the device and stays in its memory. Most reputable manufacturers still get this right; the risk is in the newer app-first entrants.

domains.name: Baby & Pet
domains.problem: The category where the cloud question stops being abstract. Wi-Fi video baby monitors have a long public history of being reached by people who should not have reached them. A DECT audio monitor removes the entire class of problem — no account to compromise, no server to breach, nothing leaving the building — at the cost of audio rather than video.

domains.name: Tools & Outdoor
domains.problem: The cheap end of weather stations and yard equipment has gone almost entirely cloud-only, with several popular products shipping no display at all and existing purely as a feed into a vendor app. The instruments that keep a local console with the database on the device are the ones still worth buying.

domains.name: Watches & Wearables
domains.problem: A watch that needs charging nightly and an account to sync is a different product from a watch. The dumb end of this category is not a compromise — a quartz digital watch keeps better time than most smartwatches and runs for a decade on one cell.

domains.name: Office & Hobby
domains.problem: Mostly a benign category, and a useful source of the third-party-certification trick: exam boards prohibit devices capable of communication, so an SAT or AP approval is an enforceable certification that a device has no radio in it.
